title: Sita
hook: a king is plowing a field, and a girl rises out of the furrow

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a season with the breath again: Bhrigu found that breath is Brahman, and his father sent him on to look further. Did you test one answer you were sure of? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

A king is plowing. Not a farmer, a king, walking behind the plow, clearing a field. And out of the furrow, out of the turned earth, a girl rises. He lifts her up, takes her home, and raises her as his own daughter. The king is Janaka of Mithila. The girl is Sita. A new season starts today: the women of the epics, heard in their own words where the texts give them words. And it starts with the one who came out of the ground.
screen: `A KING BEHIND THE PLOW.` → `A GIRL RISES FROM THE FURROW.` → `A SEASON OF THE EPICS' WOMEN.`

segments.voice: The story comes late in the first book of Valmiki's Ramayana, and it comes from Janaka's own mouth. Here it is in paraphrase. While I was plowing the field, he says, a girl rose from the earth. I found her while clearing the ground, and she is known by the name Sita. She was not born from a womb, he adds, and he calls her his daughter. Then he sets a test for any man who wants to marry her: lift and string the great bow of Shiva that sits in his house. Many have tried, he says, and failed. The rest comes in the next chapter: Rama lifts the bow, and it breaks. So here are three things to hold onto as this season begins. First, the name. Tradition hears in it the Sanskrit word for a furrow, the line the plow cuts, so her name carries the field she came from. Second, her father. The Upanishads tell of a King Janaka who loved to ask about the self, the one we heard questioning Yajnavalkya about dreams and deep sleep, and tradition links Sita's father to that king or to his line. In that telling, the girl from the furrow grows up in a house of seekers. Third, the shape of her whole story. She comes out of the earth here, at the start. In the Ramayana's last book, she goes back into it. The ground opens and takes her home. Hold both ends. The season ahead isn't about who Sita belongs to. It's about what she says and chooses, in the places where the text lets her speak.
screen: `JANAKA TELLS IT IN HIS OWN WORDS` · `THE BOW OF SHIVA` · `A NAME THAT CARRIES THE FIELD` · `FROM THE EARTH, AND BACK TO IT`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel the ground that holds you. Sit, or stand if you like, and let your weight drop. Notice exactly where the floor or the earth meets you: the feet, the seat, the hands. Let each breath out settle you a little more into it. The ground under Sita is the same ground under you, turned, planted, walked on. If you pray, you can give thanks for the earth, as some Hindus do when they touch it in the morning. Otherwise, simply rest on it. The bell holds the time.
Sita. In Valmiki, Janaka finds her rising from the earth as he plows, and tradition hears the furrow in her name. Today's word.
Your line: Sita. Today, notice the ground once, under your feet or under a plant, and remember the girl who rose out of it. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Sita is honored in Hindu devotion as a goddess and as Rama's wife, and her birth is celebrated in some communities as Sita Navami; her story is retold in Valmiki's Ramayana and in later versions such as Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas.

notes: First day of 'The epics revisited — the women' (week 39 of year four). Sarga numbers follow the vulgate (Gorakhpur) numbering; the Baroda critical edition numbers differ. Please confirm.

Bala Kanda 66: confirm Janaka's account (plowing/clearing the field; the girl rising from the earth; 'known by the name Sita'; ayonija, not womb-born). The hook says he plowed 'to make the ground ready for a sacred rite' (yajna); confirm.
'Sita means furrow': standard lexicons give sita as furrow; the lesson ties the name to the furrow, which Janaka's account implies. A Keeper should confirm the framing is not a preacher's etymology.

Janaka 'remembered in the Upanishads as a king who loved to ask about the self' (Brihadaranyaka 3–4): confirm, and that the epic's Janaka is traditionally identified with that king or with his line; soften if needed.
'Many have tried and failed' follows Janaka's speech in Bala Kanda 66; confirm.
Practice line 'as some Hindus do when they touch it in the morning' (bhumi vandana): softened to 'some'.
howItsDone: Sita Navami and 'honored by Hindus as a goddess' should be confirmed.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced 'sacred rite' from the plowing scene; fixed the garbled line 'The path has met the rest before'; cut the unverifiable 'which we read in year two'; the furrow meaning of the name is now framed as 'tradition hears' (voice, word, original, trapdoor) under the claims rule; the identification of Sita's father with the Upanishads' Janaka is now attributed to tradition, since Janaka is also a dynastic name; softened 'honored by Hindus' in howItsDone.
